hits.draft_en:
I found something nasty in a place I train and it made me rethink “clean enough.”

On sites we chase dust and diesel. At home a lot of blokes never check the air in the shed or the garage gym. Mold doesn’t care that you bought a nice rack.

I’m 63, still on telehandlers and early starts. If the room I train in is cooking my recovery, the program doesn’t matter.

Simple move this week: smell-test + look for damp, and if it’s a closed garage, get a real air check — not vibes.

Train hard. Breathe clean.
hits.video_tip: 15–25s face-to-cam in the garage gym: point at corners/ceiling, say “if the room is dirty, the program fails,” end on open the roller door.

hits.text: I do periodic mold testing at my house. I used a Buck BioAire B520. It pulls a calibrated volume of air through a spore trap cassette which slams airborne particles onto a sticky slide. The spore count is then counted using a microscope.
hits.draft_en:
Bryan Johnson actually measures mold with a calibrated air pump and a sticky slide under a microscope.

Most of us just open a window and hope.

I’m not building Blueprint. I am a 63-year-old who wants next year’s body to still climb into a telehandler.

Takeaway: what you don’t measure in the environment still hits your sleep, sinuses, and training.

One test beats ten theories.

hits.name: Paul Saladino, MD
hits.text: how to sleep through the night: -2 tablespoons honey + pinch of salt before bed (this was critical for me) -10 min sunlight first thing in am (no sunglasses!) -no blue light, no flickering light 2 hours before bed (no phones, no LED lights etc, red light in house etc.) -majority of fluids in first 10 hours of the day, minimize after that -adequate calories during the day (from high quality foods) + reasonable macros (0.8 g protein/lb goal body weight, ~25-30%+ fat cals, carbohydrates based on activity level- at least 150g daily) -magnesium prior to sleep.
hits.draft_en:
How to sleep through the night — without a 40-tab stack.

Saladino’s list that actually maps to a labour-hire week:
- Morning sun, no sunglasses, 10 minutes
- Eat enough real food in the day (protein first)
- Front-load fluids; don’t flood the bladder at 10pm
- Phone and blue light out earlier than you want
- Magnesium before bed
- His critical one: honey + pinch of salt before sleep (test it; don’t treat it like gospel)

Early starts punish bad nights. Protect the whole show.
hits.video_tip: 30–40s bedtime checklist on a whiteboard; tick three you’ll keep this week.

hits.name: Andy Galpin, PhD
hits.text: Training smarter doesn't mean lifting less. It means better programming. Physical therapist and strength coach @drjohnrusin says "longevity" has become a reason for people to back off. Someone hears the word, drops the load, drops the intensity, and slow-rolls into a program that's safe but doesn't do anything. The client stays healthy in the sense that nothing hurts, and loses the exact capacities they hired a coach to protect. Power starts declining somewhere around your early thirties, roughly 1 to 2% a year. Muscle is the same story. If you aren't actively building or keeping it, you're losing it. You still have to lift. What smarter looks like instead: - Train what declines. Muscle, strength, power. If it leaves on its own, it has to be actively kept. - Every block should work now and still hold up years from now. - Keep the challenge, change the dose. The stimulus stays. How it's loaded, sequenced, and recovered from is what gets more careful. - The principles that make someone strong, capable, and resilient don't change with the sport or the age. What changes is how you apply them. Longevity doesn't mean back off. It means be more strategic.
hits.draft_en:
“Longevity” is getting used as a soft excuse to never lift hard again.

Galpin’s crew are right: safer but useless programming keeps you comfortable and weak.

Over 50 I still need power and load — programmed smart, not vanished.

Healthy that can’t pick up a grandchild or climb a machine isn’t the goal.
hits.video_tip: 30–40s: one explosive-but-safe move + one heavy compound; caption “longevity ≠ deload forever.”

hits.name: Nick Norwitz MD PhD
hits.text: Why You Can’t Focus 🧠 🧵 1/5) New research in Cell suggests what we call “attention problems” may be sleep problems wearing a disguise. Here's the deal: stimulants like Ritalin and Vyvanse have been prescribed for ~90 years on one assumption: they turn up the brain’s “attention machinery.” But when a team at Washington University conducted fMRI brain scans on nearly 12,000 kids, and then adults on and off a stimulant, to watch what the drugs actually do inside the brain... what the found surprised me. The attention networks were untouched.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text: Ever since my research fellowship in Asia, I've been fascinated with the differences in ethnicity and body weight. One big finding: If you're of Asian descent, a "normal" BMI can still come with significant metabolic risk. BMI (body mass index; weight divided by height squared) cutoffs were built mostly on data from people of European descent. Many Asian populations develop type 2 diabetes and heart disease at lower BMIs, which is why the World Health Organization suggested lower action points for them, starting around 23 instead of 25. Better than BMI: Check your waist against your height. For most people, keeping your waist under half your height is a better guide.
hits.draft_en:
BMI can lie. Waist tells more truth.

Bikman’s point: some people — especially many of Asian descent — get metabolic trouble at a “normal” BMI. WHO even flagged lower action points.

Simple home check: keep waist under half your height.

I’m not chasing a chart on the internet. I’m chasing a waist that doesn’t fight the belt after a week of good food and lifting.

hits.name: Nick Norwitz MD PhD
hits.text: Diet Soda Debate: What Everyone (Still) Gets Wrong I recently posted some short-form content about "what everybody gets wrong about diet soda." As not only anticipated, but intended, there were split opinions. So let me use that as a springboard to clarify. And I’ll open with a question: How much of your health are you willing to gamble? What you’re seeing below are data from a human study published in Nature (PMID: 25231862). Researchers took people who didn’t normally consume artificial sweeteners and gave them non-caloric artificial sweeteners (NAS) for seven days. 4 of the 7 people developed worse glucose tolerance on an oral glucose tolerance test, which you can see below. And we have evidence that the effect was mediated by disruption of the microbiome. Researchers took microbiome samples from these people before and after artificial-sweetener exposure and effectively did poop transplants into mice. The microbiota collected after exposure could transfer the impaired glucose response to the animals. So the proposed chain of events is: Artificial sweetener → altered microbiome → impaired glucose tolerance. Quoting "Collectively, our results link non-caloric artificial sweetener (NAS) consumption, dysbiosis and metabolic abnormalities, thereby calling for a reassessment of massive NAS usage." Now, critics will correctly point out that this was a small human study coupled with mechanistic animal work. True. It’s rather difficult to do a 100,000-person interventional trial involving microbiome transplants. What we have here is precision, not scale. And that leaves a huge open question: if a little over half of participants responded adversely over just one week, how frequently does that happen in the broader population? And what differentiates responders from non-responders? We don’t know yet. So if you want to consume artificial sweeteners, go ahead. The sweetener used in this particular human experiment was saccharin, and the exact same experiment was not performed with aspartame, as found in Diet Coke. In fairness, that distinction matters. But that’s absence of evidence (re: aspartame and this singular outcome), not evidence of absence. Which brings me back to the question: What do you want to gamble? Open question. Another question is: is there a smarter choice? Like stevia, allulose, or monkfruit. My answer is yes. Another response I frequently get is people hand-waving toward large meta-analyses and trials. But look carefully at what some of these studies are comparing. The SWEET study is often cited (PMID: 41057614). But in this study artificial sweeteners are compared to a regular sugar group as a control. "One group replaced sugar-rich products with sweetness enhancers (S&SEs)." So, if you want to force a binary choice between Diet Coke and regular Coke, then okay, replacing a large amount of sugar with a non-caloric alternative may have advantages. But I think that’s a dumb binary, frankly. It's forced. It's like asking me whether I'd rather drop an anvil on my foot or stab my hand. Can't I choose neither? (It's an analogy folks - not meant to represent proportional harm.) Anyway, at the end of the day, I don’t care what you drink. Diet soda. Regular soda. Milkshakes. You're an adult. Make your own choices. Just don't be the diet soda defender who sticks their head in the sand. Thanks and have a lovely Sunday :)
hits.draft_en:
Diet soda isn’t free. Norwitz’s question is the right one: how much of your health are you willing to gamble?

Small human work linked some artificial sweeteners to worse glucose tolerance via the microbiome — not settled for every can of Diet Coke, but not nothing.

I’m not joining a soda war. I am choosing water, tea, or the odd treat on purpose — not pretending “zero calories” means zero trade-offs.
